passage: The rain had already soaked Mehak's bag when Sonali caught up with her under the bus shelter, out of breath. "I've got two minutes before my dad's car leaves," Sonali said. "I'm sorry for what I said last term. Your hair, the group chat, all of it." Mehak felt her shoulders drop, a small relief, and right behind it a hot flicker of anger. Had Sonali only come because the class teacher had spoken to her? She noticed Sonali's wet fringe and the way her fingers twisted the bag strap. "Okay," Mehak said slowly. "Thank you for saying it. I'm not ready to sit with you at lunch, though." Sonali nodded, hurt but quiet, and ran for the car. On the bus, Mehak watched the water streak down the window. She had accepted the apology. She had not forgotten a single word.

qa.q: Where did Sonali apologise to Mehak?
qa.a: Under the bus shelter, in the rain.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Mehak have when Sonali apologised, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Relief and anger, with some doubt. Her shoulders dropped, a hot flicker of anger came right after, and she wondered if Sonali had come only because the class teacher had spoken to her.

qa.q: What would you advise Mehak about lunch and about Sonali from here on?
qa.a: Keep the boundary she set, stay polite, and give herself time. Accepting an apology does not mean trusting again straight away, and she can tell a teacher if the mocking starts again. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt as she ran for the car?
qa.a: Probably hurt but also aware she had to earn back trust. She nodded quietly instead of arguing, and her fingers had twisted the strap while she apologised, which suggests nerves.

grounding: Mehak accepts the bully's apology with mixed relief, doubt and anger while keeping a boundary.

passage: Anjali, put the phone down a minute. You say Mr Bose's class is pointless because he picks on you. I said the same at fifteen about my chemistry teacher, Mrs Dias. Your Nani Elizabeth was no saint then. She asked me the hardest questions, and I was sure she wanted me to fail, so I stopped doing her homework and sat sulking on the back bench. Two terms of marks slipped away. Then I began writing things down: the date, what she asked, what she said. When I read the list, half of it looked less unfair than I'd thought. The other half still stung. So I asked to speak to her after school and told her plainly how it felt. She was surprised. She didn't turn into an angel, but she dropped the sharpest remarks. And I had to work to win my marks back, because the marks were mine, not hers.

qa.q: What did young Elizabeth write down in her list about Mrs Dias?
qa.a: The date, what she asked, and what she said.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth stop doing Mrs Dias's homework?
qa.a: She felt targeted by the hardest questions and was sure Mrs Dias wanted her to fail, so resentment made her stop trying.

qa.q: What would you advise Anjali to do about Mr Bose's class?
qa.a: Note down specific examples, ask him for a private talk, and keep doing the work, since the marks are hers either way.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dias have seen the private talk?
qa.a: With surprise. That suggests she hadn't realised how her remarks landed, and afterwards she dropped the sharpest ones.

grounding: An elder recalls resenting a teacher, sulking, then gathering examples, talking privately and working on.

passage: Ganga, you asked why I keep that scratched geometry box. Sit. When I was fourteen, my maths teacher Mr Kulkarni stopped at my desk and said, "Tushar, you can top the district if you want it." Nobody had said anything like that to me. I worked till the lamp oil ran low, just to see him nod. Then, in class ten, he was transferred to another town. I panicked. For a week I opened no book, as if the belief had left in his bus. My Dada finally asked, "Was it his nodding you studied for, or the sums?" That question stayed with me. I made my own timetable and marked my own mistakes. I still wrote to Mr Kulkarni when my results came. But I didn't need his answer to know whether I had tried.

qa.q: What did Mr Kulkarni say to Tushar when he was fourteen?
qa.a: He said, "Tushar, you can top the district if you want it."

qa.q: Why did Tushar stop opening his books for a week after Mr Kulkarni was transferred?
qa.a: He felt as if the belief had left with the teacher. His drive had depended on seeing Mr Kulkarni nod, so he felt lost.

qa.q: What could a student do to use a teacher's belief without depending on it?
qa.a: Work hard for the subject and set their own goals and timetable, so effort does not vanish if the teacher's approval does. 👍

qa.q: How might Mr Kulkarni have felt receiving Tushar's letter?
qa.a: Likely glad and proud, since Tushar still wrote to him. Tushar also no longer needed his answer, so the teacher's belief had helped him grow rather than tied him down.

grounding: A teacher's belief motivates the protagonist, who then builds his own drive beyond approval.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta,

Promise you won't laugh. Ever since Mr Rao started reading poems aloud in English, my stomach does a little flip when he walks in. I sit up straight, I know every answer, and yesterday when he said "good" to me I nearly floated home. It's the best and most embarrassing feeling ever. 😅 I even started a poem for him, then tore it into tiny pieces and put it in the bin under the tissues. Remember you told me about your tuition-sir crush last year, and how it just faded? I'm hanging onto that. I'm not going to give him anything or write him notes. It's mine, and it stays in this letter. Kabir from debate club asked to borrow my notes, so maybe I'll be a bit nicer to him. Tell me it's normal!

Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do with the poem she started for Mr Rao?
qa.a: She tore it into tiny pieces and put it in the bin under the tissues.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi feel about her feelings for Mr Rao, and what shows it?
qa.a: She finds them thrilling but embarrassing. Her stomach flips when he walks in, she nearly floated home after his "good", and she asks Sangeeta not to laugh.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi choose to do about her crush, and why is it a sensible choice?
qa.a: She keeps it private and gives Mr Rao no notes, hoping it fades like Sangeeta's did. That avoids an awkward situation, and she can turn her attention toward classmates her own age.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably fond and understanding, since she had a similar crush that faded. She may also feel trusted, because Lakshmi shares something so private with her.

grounding: The protagonist describes a thrilling crush on a teacher and chooses to keep it private and not act on it.

passage: Every morning Lavanya carried the Hindi register from the staffroom to Class Nine, because Madam Sushila had asked her to. In the small-town school by the bus stand, that was enough for whispers. "Madam ji ki chamchi," someone muttered, and Sarika copied Lavanya's walk, chin up, to laughter. Lavanya's ears burned, but she only put the register on the desk. At break, she saw Sarika staring at a fractions sum on her slate. Lavanya thought of saying "I always get full marks, look" and swallowed it. Instead she sat down beside her. "Want me to show you the trick my mother taught me?" Sarika shrugged, then slid the slate over. Nothing was said about the walk. But next morning a space on the bench was kept for Lavanya, and Sarika's bag was not on it.

qa.q: What did Lavanya carry to Class Nine every morning?
qa.a: The Hindi register from the staffroom.

qa.q: What did Lavanya want to say to Sarika at break, and why did she swallow it?
qa.a: She thought of saying "I always get full marks, look", which would have shown off and belittled Sarika. She swallowed it because she did not want to be smug.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do well in handling the teasing?
qa.a: She stayed humble and offered to help Sarika with the sum instead of using her place with the teacher to look down on anyone.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Lavanya after the break?
qa.a: She seems to soften. She slid the slate over and next morning kept a space on the bench, so she may now see Lavanya as a friendly classmate rather than a chamchi.

grounding: A teacher's pet stays humble under teasing and helps a classmate instead of belittling her.

passage: "Irfan, you haven't touched your roti." "Not hungry, Pooja apa." "Since when? What happened?" "Mr Verma. In Maths. I got the answer wrong and he said, in front of everybody, 'Sit down, you're useless, you'll never amount to anything.' Everyone laughed." "And what did you do?" "Nothing. My face was burning. I wanted to shout at him. I just sat there and stared at the desk." "That took strength, you know." "It doesn't feel like it. I feel stupid." "A wrong answer is a wrong answer. What he said was about him, not you. Tell Abbu tonight." "He'll say don't make trouble." "He'll listen. And if it happens again, we go to the vice principal, together." Irfan picked up the roti at last. 🤍

qa.q: What did Mr Verma say to Irfan in front of the class?
qa.a: "Sit down, you're useless, you'll never amount to anything."

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling in the classroom, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Shame and rage. His face was burning and he wanted to shout at the teacher, but he sat there staring at the desk.

qa.q: What would you advise Irfan to do next?
qa.a: Tell Abbu tonight, remember the insult says something about the teacher's conduct and not his worth, and report it to the vice principal if it repeats. 🤍

qa.q: How does Pooja see what happened in the classroom?
qa.a: She sees Irfan's silence as strength, not weakness. She thinks the words reflect on the teacher, and she wants to stand with him if it happens again.

grounding: A teenager humiliated by a teacher stays composed, tells a family member and plans to report if it repeats.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9.

Gopika was referred by her class teacher after going blank when called on in physics. In our talk she said she freezes as soon as Mr Arnab enters, her hands go cold, and she avoids his eyes. I asked whether he has ever mocked anyone. She thought and said no; he only expects homework done and silence during explanation. We talked about how strict and cruel are different things. Together we made a small plan: revise the day's topic a little longer the night before, and ask him one question a week, written down beforehand. Last Friday she asked about a diagram. Mr Arnab answered plainly and said "good question." She reported that her voice shook but she got the words out. I will check in again after the exam.

qa.q: What small plan did Gopika and the counsellor make?
qa.a: To revise the day's topic a little longer the night before and to ask Mr Arnab one written question a week.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when Mr Arnab entered the room, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was scared. Her hands went cold, she avoided his eyes and she froze when he called on her.

qa.q: Why does the counsellor talk with Gopika about strict versus cruel?
qa.a: So she can see that Mr Arnab is demanding but has never mocked anyone, which makes him easier to approach. A teacher who was cruel would call for telling an adult instead.

qa.q: How might Mr Arnab see Gopika's question about the diagram?
qa.a: Likely as a welcome sign of interest. He answered plainly and said "good question", so he seems glad a quiet student spoke up.

grounding: A student afraid of a strict teacher prepares more and asks one question a week, separating strictness from cruelty.

passage:
Day one. Ms Ritu handed back Kalyani's essay with red ink on nearly every line. "Again," was all she said. Kalyani stuffed it into her bag, cheeks hot, thinking Ms Ritu enjoyed this.

Two weeks later. Fourth draft. Ms Ritu read it standing at the desk. "Now it says what you mean." It wasn't praise exactly, but Kalyani walked out taller than she'd walked in.

Six years later. In her first-year seminar, the professor read out Kalyani's paragraph as a model. That evening she visited her old school and found Ms Ritu in the staffroom. "Thank you for all that red ink," she said. Ms Ritu laughed, then grew serious. "I was too sharp with some of your classmates. It worked for you. It doesn't always." Kalyani nodded. She knew a friend who had stopped writing altogether.

qa.q: How many drafts did Kalyani write before Ms Ritu said "Now it says what you mean"?
qa.a: Four drafts.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling on the first day when she stuffed her essay into her bag?
qa.a: Anger and hurt. Her cheeks were hot and she thought Ms Ritu enjoyed marking so harshly.

qa.q: What should Kalyani take from Ms Ritu's remark that being sharp worked for her but doesn't always?
qa.a: That harshness helping her once does not make it right for everyone. She can thank Ms Ritu while still seeing that some students, like her friend, may be hurt by it.

qa.q: How does Ms Ritu see her own teaching years later?
qa.a: With some doubt. She admits she was too sharp with some students, so she sees that what worked for Kalyani did not work for everyone.

grounding: Years later the protagonist thanks a hard teacher while recognising that harshness is not always good.

passage:
I sit behind Rekha in Civics, so I saw it all. Mr Sen was checking notebooks, and hers was missing the last assignment. "Careless, lazy, and probably proud of it," he said, loud enough for the whole room. A few people laughed. Rekha's ears went red. She stared at her desk and didn't answer. I can't say what she was thinking; she just held her pen very still. At break she went and stood alone in the corridor. Next morning she told me she had written down what he said, the date and who was sitting near her. Her father was coming to meet the coordinator. She asked if I'd tell them what I heard. I said yes. I don't know if that helps, but she nodded, and her shoulders looked a little less tight.

Charu, Class 9

qa.q: What did Mr Sen say about Rekha's missing assignment?
qa.a: He said "Careless, lazy, and probably proud of it" loud enough for the whole room.

qa.q: What did Rekha's behaviour after the remark suggest she was feeling, according to Charu?
qa.a: Charu can't be sure, but the red ears, the stillness and the walk to the corridor alone suggest shame. Her silence could also mean she was too shaken to answer.

qa.q: What could Charu do to support Rekha?
qa.a: Tell the coordinator what she heard if asked, stay friendly with Rekha, and not gossip about it. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Charu said yes to being a witness?
qa.a: Probably relieved not to be alone with it. She nodded and her shoulders looked a little less tight, which suggests the support mattered.

grounding: An observer describes a classmate publicly shamed by a teacher and her response of keeping a record and telling a parent.

passage:
Principal's note.

Jahnavi (Class 10) asked to see me on Tuesday, with her friend Rafiq beside her and her mother's permission. She was nervous but organised. She had dated notes: twice the maths teacher had refused to recheck her total and told her to stop questioning. She stuck to what happened and did not name motives. She told me she hadn't posted anything anywhere; she wanted the school to look at it first. Rafiq confirmed he had seen the second incident. I thanked them both and said I would go through the paper myself and speak to the teacher. I found an addition slip of several marks and have corrected it. I will meet the teacher about how students' queries are answered, and see Jahnavi again in a couple of weeks to ask if things feel different.

qa.q: Who came with Jahnavi to see the principal?
qa.a: Her friend Rafiq.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi want by going to the school first instead of posting online?
qa.a: She wanted the school to look at it and fix it, so she trusted that the proper route would work.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi's approach of dated notes and facts make it easier to solve?
qa.a: It gave the principal something clear to check. Sticking to what happened and not guessing motives let them find the addition slip and correct it.

qa.q: How does the principal seem to see Jahnavi's report?
qa.a: As a serious, responsible step. They thanked both students, checked the paper themselves and planned to meet the teacher and follow up with Jahnavi.

grounding: A student reports unfair treatment through the proper route, factually and with a friend, and gives it time.
